verdicts.explanation: Neither page cites a recorded test. The access setup says its one probe that day was 'inconclusive only because Wolters Kluwer refuses plain clients outright'. The overnight report shows the refetch went through the proxy session instead.
verdicts.resolution_hint: Record a probe (PMC from the grid against WSL, and one publisher from the grid IP) before the book states either claim. Otherwise state only the route that ran: WSL plus the WSU proxy.

verdicts.topic: The printed label beside the vertebra is the strongest anchor
verdicts.quote_a: authors print 'L4' beside the vertebra; the strongest anchor there is, and a pointer to vertebrae the detector missed
verdicts.quote_b: The caption's "L4" was, in most figures, assigned by the author counting on a limited field.
verdicts.explanation: The map's claim has no source. The reality check's sentence is about the caption's level, not a printed label, but both are levels the author assigned by counting. The reality check also calls printed level labels (3.6% of 2,815 scanned panels) a leak a network will learn. The audit's script data gives printed-level OCR 53.8% caption-held-out containment on n = 13, below figure mates, captions, the VLM and hardware. That is the only measurement, and as far as it goes it contradicts 'strongest'.
verdicts.resolution_hint: Drop 'strongest anchor' unless a read measures how accurate printed labels are. Cite the audit's 53.8% (n = 13) as the only measurement, and call it agreement, not accuracy.

verdicts.topic: A whole-run-correct panel should be the common case on the level verification bench
verdicts.quote_a: Use a to mark every box on a panel right when the whole run is correct, which should be the common case and makes this fast.
verdicts.quote_b: the level model alone is the weakest term in the decoder on real panels (37.9% on 169)
verdicts.explanation: Nothing measured supports the bench's expectation. The reality check's figures do not prove the opposite either: they come from a selected caption-free subset and measure containment or a single decider, not whether a whole run is correct on a random sample. Still, the expectation has no basis, and the one-key shortcut invites readers to accept the model's names.
verdicts.resolution_hint: Remove 'which should be the common case' from the bench instructions, or replace it with the measured rate once the bench has reads.

the lab recipe's two-member CephFS group and the 0 of 79 job-id keys are as of 2026-09-27; the onboarding (2026-10-13) leaves issue 19 open on whether the grid reaches GitHub and sends students to an archive the connect note (2026-10-14) says is not filled yet; the reforms checklist (2026-10-03) names framework 11 and extension 12.0.0 and says none of its gates exists yet, while the 2026-10-21 plan and review name framework 22 and Beethoven 23.x with no second worker started and only the Wayne State account signed in; the brief (2026-10-14) says nothing after 0.4.1 is released and F8 is open; the registry (2026-10-20) marks VinDr's determination pending, requests 1 to 14 never sent, no bank built for the geometry solved 2026-09-23, and sample counts empty until a grid job runs; the grid pipeline (2026-10-21) has gate words under review in PR #54, no job run, 5 of 20 recipes ready, 22 registry entries with no shard, 26 requested and 5 granted in spine-datasets, CT-RATE off by the owner's decision of 21 October, the RSNA RATIC link expiring 2026-10-28 02:38 UTC, one press remaining for the owner, and a schedule of 25 October (frames drawn), 28 October (version 1 trained), 30 October (provisional filed) and 2 November (CNS mini-oral 66629); the any-view plan (2026-10-21) has the census job built in PR #76 and not yet run; the AIDAS proposal's deadline of 16 October 2026 has passed with no record of submission; and the September pages (counting-from-the-sacrum, the board) describe a training run and an audit as running, and the IRB files as public, both overtaken by the decisions page.
result.notes: All 19 records were read in full; the plain texts were searched once for the duplicated board/decisions sentences, the afterany rule, DysphagiaBank and the 4.3-point figure, and the extraction's line breaks and characters made every pattern but one miss, so verbatim duplicate findings rest on the records' quote fields rather than on the texts. Two facts loaded into this session from the repositories' own memory, not from the records, bear on candidates and are left out of them: SchwingNet's memory says WSU IRB HPR 2026-330 of 29 September 2026 covers VinDr-SpineXR under its PhysioNet agreement, which would make the registry's 'determination pending' line stale; and the fetch-chain memory says each fetch refuses to exceed the volume's free space minus 1 TB where the grid pipeline artifact says minus 5 TB. The repository's PROTOCOL.md now dates idleness by the push GitHub received, which resolves the F8 candidate in the review's favour; that too is outside the records. People are named by role throughout; the owner's first name appears inside quoted text where the record carried it. No e-mail address, phone number or home address appears in any record quoted. The cluster is confidential patent material by the any-view plan's and the project goal's own words.

result.cluster: Symphony: the protocol, its evidence and its place (part symphony-beethoven)

candidates.topic: Whether Symphony has any hosted piece of its own (the 'no server' claim)
candidates.statement_a: Symphony has nothing to host: no server, database or daemon of the project's own (2026-10-15).
candidates.quote_a: There is nothing to host. No server, database or daemon of the project's own
candidates.statement_b: The product has a webhook server (symphony-app, undeployed, to be deleted) and an approved but unbuilt Cloudflare sign-in service for the control panel (2026-10-13).
candidates.quote_b: Hosted pieces: nothing of ours runs. The webhook server is not deployed, and the Cloudflare sign-in service is approved but not built
candidates.why_it_matters: 'No server' holds for the claim protocol only; a planner who reads the spec alone would not budget, secure or review the stateless sign-in service the control panel depends on, nor know the webhook stage still exists in symphony-app's code until its deletion lands.

candidates.topic: Whether coordination in Actions with no server distinguishes Symphony
candidates.statement_a: The headline design claim is a serverless protocol in which git lets exactly one of two racing creations win.
candidates.quote_a: with no server of its own... git lets exactly one of two racing creations win
candidates.statement_b: The spec's own list of what not to claim says serverless coordination in Actions is shared by unsorry and gh-aw.
candidates.quote_b: Coordination that runs in Actions with no server: unsorry and gh-aw do it too.
candidates.why_it_matters: A grant or comparison that leads with 'serverless' as the distinction over-claims; only the combination of five mechanisms is claimed unique (competitors l.98 and manual l.243 agree with the spec, the opening sentence does not).

candidates.topic: Whether a subscription setup-token is sanctioned for shared CI use
candidates.statement_a: The setup-token is a one-year credential sanctioned for CI from the cheapest paid plan up (2026-10-09).
candidates.quote_a: Claude Pro's setup-token (a one-year OAuth credential, sanctioned for CI from the cheapest paid plan up) powers both @claude mentions and the scheduled worker
candidates.statement_b: Anthropic documents the token but advises an API key for a secret shared across repositories, and whether several workers on one plan are ordinary individual usage is open (R6).
candidates.quote_b: Anthropic advises an API key for a secret shared across repositories and says plan limits 'assume ordinary, individual usage'
candidates.why_it_matters: The ladder's bottom rung prices the whole machine on one Pro token in CI; the spec and the competitors note grade that usage Open, so the $17 rung may not be an approved configuration for an organization secret shared by workers.

candidates.topic: Pooling several accounts' tokens to widen the usage window
candidates.statement_a: Pooling several users' tokens or rotating accounts is the behaviour Anthropic's terms prohibit; more window means an API key.
candidates.quote_a: Rotating accounts or pooling several users' tokens to widen the window is the behaviour Anthropic's terms prohibit; if the workload needs more than one subscription's window, it is a workload for an API key.
candidates.statement_b: The owner's accounts form one pool of organization secrets picked by code, then CooperBench runs on it (decision of 2026-10-13, 'knowing the terms question').
candidates.quote_b: one organization secret per account, SYMPHONY_CLAUDE_<NAME>... SYMPHONY_CLAUDE_ACCOUNTS
candidates.why_it_matters: A planner reading the playbook would refuse the pool; one reading the handoff would build it (and the repository's memory index of 2026-10-22 says the token pool is built). The handoff limits it to the owner's own accounts and asks that the Usage Policy be re-read before 2026-11-12; the playbook makes no such allowance.

candidates.topic: GITHUB_TOKEN's hourly request limit that binds the board and benchmark
candidates.statement_a: 1,000 requests an hour per repository, with no retry on 429 (risk 5).
candidates.quote_a: GITHUB_TOKEN gets 1,000 requests an hour per repository and the library has no retry on 429
candidates.statement_b: 1,000 an hour, but 15,000 on Enterprise Cloud, and the organization is inferred to be on Enterprise Cloud.
candidates.quote_b: GITHUB_TOKEN is limited to 1,000 API requests an hour per repository, 15,000 on Enterprise Cloud
candidates.why_it_matters: The spec, manual and competitors note say the 1,000 limit probably binds before minutes (R3); if the organization is Enterprise Cloud as the handoff infers (l.47, l.1566), the binding limit is 15x higher and the scale ceiling they warn of is wrong for this organization, though right for an adopter on Free.

candidates.topic: Which GitHub plan the project itself runs on
candidates.statement_a: The bottom rung is a personal account: $17 a month for Claude, $0 guaranteed GitHub bill, GitHub Pro at $4 if private.
candidates.quote_a: $17 a month runs the whole machine... $0 is the guaranteed GitHub bill... 3,000... on both the $4 GitHub Pro plan and the GitHub Team plan
candidates.statement_b: sdlc-template is internal, so the enterprise is an Enterprise Cloud account; Code Security was not bought as of 2026-10-08.
candidates.quote_b: sdlc-template is internal (Symphony constraint) and internal visibility belongs to organizations owned by an enterprise account, so the enterprise OpenGrid is an Enterprise Cloud account; GitHub Code Security was not bought as of 2026-10-08
candidates.why_it_matters: The ladder's per-feature prices describe an adopter, not the owner's organization; a planner costing the owner's own runs (50,000 included minutes, 15,000 token requests, merge queue on private repositories) would read the wrong rung.

candidates.topic: Billed minutes saved by the board's six-hourly cron fallback
candidates.statement_a: Cutting the board's cron from hourly to six-hourly saves about 630 billed minutes a month (750 to 120).
candidates.quote_a: the board's cron fallback cut from hourly to six-hourly, saving a private repository about 630 billed minutes a month
candidates.statement_b: Schedules ran hours late and dropped most slots: the hourly board cron ran 16 of about 87 slots, the ten-minute sweep 8 of about 300.
candidates.quote_b: Schedules are best effort. Measured here, they ran hours late and dropped most slots. Every cron in the design is affected
candidates.why_it_matters: The ladder's savings are computed on slots that never ran; and the handoff's measurement means the six-hourly fallback cannot be relied on to release idle claims or refresh the board on time, which the protocol's Release section assumes.

candidates.topic: Status of the F8 fix (idle clock read from GitHub's push record, symphony-protocol#35)

candidates.quote_a: A fix that reads GitHub's own record of the push is written but not merged (finding F8)

candidates.quote_b: by the head's committer date in 0.4.1 and in every copy today, by GitHub's record of the push on main since #35 of 2026-10-15, unreleased
candidates.why_it_matters: The spec (risk 13: 'The unmerged F8 fix') and manual were written the same day #35 merged; a planner reading them would count F8 open and the defect count at 'one waits on the owner', while the competitors note counts it merged (twelve fixes on main). Every adopted copy still reads the committer date until 0.5.0 is published.

candidates.topic: Whether the protocol's validation is exhaustive or bounded
candidates.statement_a: The shipped code is checked exhaustively through every interleaving of scripted workers.
candidates.quote_a: **The shipped protocol code is checked exhaustively.** A validation harness drives the shipped library through every interleaving of scripted workers
candidates.statement_b: It is bounded checking of small worlds, not a proof; the deeper searches are the unmerged deep lane.
candidates.quote_b: This is bounded checking of small worlds, not a proof. The deeper searches and the real-git world are the deep lane, symphony-protocol#21, still unmerged
candidates.why_it_matters: 'Exhaustively' invites the reading that the protocol is proved; the brief and the spec's own grades say the search is exhaustive only within a depth and a worker count, and the real-git and github.com behaviour (R4) is not covered.

The brief (2026-10-14) is the one artifact that tallies the seventeen guarantees and names which lane checks each; it is canonical for that, though its numbers (59 mutants, depth 5, F8 open, deep lane unmerged) are the oldest in the cluster and the spec and competitors note carry the later ones.

Dated 2026-10-16, it is the latest word on the validation numbers (twelve fixes on main, 109 mutants, #35 merged, the guard's directory bug) and the only one that withdraws the 8-pair coordbench figures; it overlaps the spec heavily on CooperBench and prior art and should be read for the 'what not to claim' list.

The spec is the source the manual, the competitors note and the brief cite by section; it alone grades each claim (Verified, Inferred, Reported, Open) and lists the risks and research questions. Its one weakness is that it reports the 8-pair pass counts that the competitors note later calls not reportable.

It is the reader's guide to the spec and adds the verification passes (verify/02's three findings, the adversarial search of 25 systems) that the spec summarises; it duplicates the spec's figures rather than superseding them, so it is canonical as the method record, not as a number source.

The handoff (2026-10-13) is the only record of the decisions of that night (the pool, the runtime, the QA gate, spine-program's state, the measured dropped cron slots, the plan ladder's unconfirmed $4 prices) and says itself its state lines were not rechecked against GitHub; it is canonical for decisions and dated state, not for numbers the later three artifacts moved. The ladder (2026-10-09), left non-canonical, is nonetheless the cluster's only pricing source with a verification date and should be read beside it.

result.unsourced_summary: The cluster asserts several load-bearing claims with no source opened. The taxonomy spec (SchwingNet/symphony-and-beethoven-taxonomy-spec-lcbqro) and the competitors note (symphony-template/symphony-versus-competitors-lynwzk) both carry Cursor's report that naive locks collapsed 20 agents to the throughput of two or three and a 2026 noise-floor study putting single-seed gains under about 15 points inside noise; both are graded Reported and unnamed, the competitors note says no primary source was opened for either, and the brief (symphony-template/symphony-in-brief-9cdciz) says its Cursor row is from memory because cursor.com is blocked. The spec's argument that GitHub's free public minutes are alone in the market rests on four withdrawal dates (Travis 2020, GitLab 2021, Azure DevOps 2026 and 2027, Cirrus 2026-06-01) of which it verifies two and the manual (symphony-template/symphony-and-beethoven-taxonomy-manual-re4jtx) still asks a pass to confirm, plus a CircleCI credit cap 'Reported, from its pricing page by search'. The spec appends 'Self-hosted runners are free on every plan' to a cited quote without a citation of its own, and its risk 3 (the account reached its weekly limit on 2026-10-15) and risk 9 (Wayne State's approval, no BAA on a personal plan, Remote Control under HIPAA) link no record. The atomic claim on github.com is stated as fact by the shared plan (symphony-template/shared-multi-account-claude-project-plan-rqzwh9), the build plan (symphony-template/sdlc-build-plan-bjzikn) and the brief while the spec's R4 leaves it open, the canary's C7 runs by hand and the manual's verify/02 ran on a scratch repository. 'Branch protection on a private repository needs a paid plan' is sourced to a docs page in the shared plan, marked 'to be checked, not assumed' in the build plan and attributed to 'document 25' in the primitives spec (symphony-template/sdlc-primitives-spec-ldx4zd), and no artifact records the check. The grid review (symphony-template/grid-and-cloud-claude-workers-review) and the handoff (symphony-template/symphony-handoff) use a 90-minute cloud-worker limit, a seven-day window for remote-control --continue and 'six 90-minute runs' per schedule without saying where they were read; the shared plan's 'hooks are not loaded in a Project with several repos' and its February 2026 ban reports (a blog's guess, unconfirmed by Anthropic) are likewise untested here. The ladder (symphony-template/the-dollar-per-feature-ladder-9ymg61) alone gives Windows 1.7x and macOS 10x runner multipliers and 'about a minute per pull request event', the figure its whole monthly-minute arithmetic rests on. The handoff could not confirm the GitHub Pro and Team $4 prices the ladder says it verified, and its 'enterprise OpenGrid' name has no source.
result.stale_summary: Everything in the cluster is dated 2026-10-03 to 2026-10-16 except the two grid notes read on 21 October, and much of it is 'as of' or 'not yet'. Release state: the brief (10-14), spec (10-15), manual (10-15) and competitors note (10-16) all say 0.4.1 of 2026-10-13 is the last release and an adopter waits for 0.5.0; the template's own memory index of 2026-10-22 says the template vendors 0.5.0, merged in the library and awaiting the owner's approval, so whether it is published must be re-read. The brief's guarantee tally is 'today (b5f098d)' and predates the F8 merge (#35, 2026-10-15) and the push guard's git -C directory bug found the same day; the spec and manual call the F8 fix unmerged on the day it merged. The deep lane symphony-protocol#21 is 'still unmerged' in the brief; the canary is 'not adopted yet' and C7 runs by hand. The brief's 'overlaps by file name only' and the spec's 'overlap detection by file' predate the symbol-level Locks and overlap check (switch at advise since 2026-10-20, per the template's PROTOCOL.md as loaded). The spec's and competitors' 'Not built: the qa check, the cap of 10 runs, the public runtime, the control panel, the account pool' is partly out of date: the memory index describes the control panel and the token pool as existing. The handoff (10-13) says its claims were not rechecked against GitHub; its pending list (Beethoven 20.0.0 to the store, beethoven-qa tags v4.0.0 and v5.0.0, the webhook stage to delete, the Cloudflare sign-in service approved but not built, the Actions box ticked by Symphony Setup) and its recommendation to keep the up-to-date-branch rule are superseded by the memory's 2026-10-20 rules (SymphonyBoard applies settings via settings.yml with Symphony Setup as fallback; the up-to-date rule off everywhere). The ladder (10-09) names the repository sdlc-template, prices verified 2026-10-09, a CLAUDE_WORKER switch and a 103-agent run, and computes savings on cron slots the handoff later measured as mostly dropped; Claude Enterprise's price 'could not be verified'. The shared plan's Linear queue, routine coordinator and hourly schedule were replaced on 2026-10-09. Beethoven versions move through the cluster: hpcworker framework 11 (REFORMS checklist) to 22-23 (grid notes, 21 Oct); extension 12.0.0 to 20.0.0 (handoff, spec) to 23.x (several-grid-workers); beethoven-qa v2.0.0 tagged 2026-10-07 (encapsulated) to v3.0.0 last tag with main at 5.0.0 (handoff), while the memory index expects 6.0.0 or later. 'None of the REFORMS gates exists' (checklist) became 'one module, splits.py' (spec) and SchwingNet's memory now describes a split check in CI; Metaflow is 'chosen, not built' in the spec and manual while SchwingNet's memory describes tools/flow.py submitting Slurm jobs. The coordbench picture is three days of moving state (one coop smoke pair, then 8 pairs with 6 of 8, then those 40 runs 'not reportable' with 11 spoiled), a chosen full run of 35 new pairs whose execution is not in the records, and the owner's hold on its numbers. The grid review says no second worker has started and the Wayne State Max account is the only one signed in (21 Oct); the onboarding (10-13) tells students to wait on issue 19 for whether the grid can reach GitHub, which a Beethoven session answered on 2026-10-14. Pending dates fall due soon after 2026-10-22: pull_request_target blocked by default on public repositories from 2026-11-02, Anthropic's Usage Policy clause on routing through consumer subscriptions on 2026-11-12 (the handoff asks that it be re-read before then), ubuntu-latest to 26.04 with Python 3.14.4 in November 2026, bare mode becoming claude -p's default (date unstated), Azure DevOps turning existing public projects private in 2027, and GitHub Code Security 'not bought as of 2026-10-08'.
result.notes: All seventeen records were read whole and the plain texts grepped for every quote; quotes are copied from the text files (a few long lines are cut at a clause boundary, and one brief line carrying a redaction marker inside a commit hash was avoided). Dates in 'why it matters' come from the records' own headers. Where a candidate says what the repository looks like on 2026-10-22, the source is the CLAUDE.md, PROTOCOL.md and memory index loaded into this session as project instructions (not the inventory records), and each such use is named as 'the memory index' or 'PROTOCOL.md as loaded'; nothing was filled from general memory. The clustering gave no superseded or duplicate relations, so the canonical_check records agreement with the five canonical ids and why, and suggests the ladder be read beside them as the only dated price source. The artifact symphony-template/claude-chat-vs-claude-code-architectural-analysis-snuzfd carries no Symphony claim (it compares the chat and Claude Code surfaces) and yielded no candidate; symphony-template/beethoven-build-roadmap-sttvvw and SchwingNet/reforms-compliance-checklist-bpzdoi are from 2026-10-03 and predate the protocol, so their candidates concern Beethoven's engine and gates only. The two grid notes (grid-and-cloud-claude-workers-review, several-grid-workers-one-per-project) were read on 21 October, after the cluster's stated 13-16 October window, and are the freshest state in the cluster. Three candidates have artifact_b equal to artifact_a (an internal inconsistency in the handoff's copy count, the shared plan's hooks claim, and the ladder's own run-time figure); the schema allows that for stale and unsourced kinds, and the handoff case is marked contradiction because the two statements sit in one document. candidates.topic: The work queue: Linear or GitHub Issues
candidates.statement_a: The plan of 2026-10-08 makes Linear the queue, with states Todo, Claimed, In review and Done and a label per account; the claim branch is named after the Linear issue (claude/LIN-123).
candidates.quote_a: Linear holds the work queue and the conversation about each task.
candidates.statement_b: On 2026-10-09 the owner chose GitHub Issues as the queue and deferred Linear; every later artifact (the ladder, the brief, the taxonomy, the onboarding) has issues as the queue and claude/N as the branch.
candidates.quote_b: On 2026-10-09 [the owner] chose GitHub Issues and asked for the repository side first, as a GitHub template repository built from the bottom up with no export or import in its first layer (the sdlc-template work in the same thread); Linear and the materializer come later.
candidates.why_it_matters: A planner reading only the 2026-10-08 plan would set up a Linear team, a Claimed state and LIN-numbered branches; Symphony's claim lock, board and release all read GitHub issue numbers, and the Linear connector was never wired.

candidates.topic: Who releases an idle claim: a routine on the main account or the board's own run
candidates.statement_a: The coordinator is a routine on the owner's main account, woken by PR events, pushes to main and an hourly schedule, acting as that account.
candidates.quote_a: The coordinator is a routine on your main account, so it acts as that account.
candidates.statement_b: By 2026-10-14 releasing idle claims and overlap notices are a code step inside the board's own GitHub Actions run on the repository token, costing no Claude usage; only epic planning is Claude.
candidates.quote_b: A coordinator step in that same run frees claims idle for 24 hours and tells overlapping work which lands first; Claude splits large requests (epics) into tasks.
candidates.why_it_matters: The release mechanism's trust and cost differ: a routine spends one account's plan and depends on that account's routine caps and schedule, while the board step runs on GITHUB_TOKEN and needs no Claude account; the student onboarding of 2026-10-13 already describes the board's run.

candidates.topic: The board's schedule fallback: hourly or six-hourly
candidates.statement_a: The coordinator runs once an hour, and the hourly run catches a missed event within the hour.
candidates.quote_a: a routine on your main account that wakes on PR events, on every push to main (through a small GitHub Action) and once an hour
candidates.statement_b: On 2026-10-09 the board's cron fallback was cut from hourly to six-hourly to save about 630 billed minutes a month on a private repository; the brief and the taxonomy both say every six hours.
candidates.quote_b: the board's cron fallback cut from hourly to six-hourly, saving a private repository about 630 billed minutes a month
candidates.why_it_matters: The plan's promise that a dropped event is caught within the hour no longer holds; a missed event now waits up to six hours (or longer, see the cron measurement), which changes how soon a claim is released or a board entry appears.

candidates.topic: Whether GitHub's scheduled runs actually fire (the cost and the catch-up arithmetic)
candidates.statement_a: The ladder prices the board fallback as if every cron slot runs: about 750 minutes a month hourly, about 120 six-hourly, a 630-minute saving.
candidates.quote_a: the six-hourly board fallback (about 120 minutes a month, cut from about 750 when it was hourly)
candidates.statement_b: The handoff measured that GitHub ran only 16 of about 87 hourly slots on the test repository's board cron and 8 of about 300 ten-minute slots on the sweep, with gaps of 3.4 to 9 hours, and concludes that every timing claim built on a cron does not hold.
candidates.quote_b: sdlc-template-test board.yml (cron '17 * * * *') 16 scheduled runs from 2026-10-09T09:11Z to 2026-10-13T00:42Z (~87 slots)
candidates.why_it_matters: The 630-minute saving and the plan's within-the-hour catch-up are both overestimates of what a cron delivers; an experiment that relies on the schedule as a timing guarantee, or budgets minutes from it, would be wrong by a factor of about five.

canonical_check.why: The build plan records the owner's choice of 2026-10-09 (GitHub Issues, repository side first) that overturns the plan's Linear queue, LIN-numbered branches and Claimed state, and replaces the routine coordinator with a board Action; but the build plan itself centres on the cswap materializer route, which the same choice deferred and no later artifact reports built, and it does not restate the plan's nine setup steps, failure-mode table or the February 2026 ban warning. For the protocol as it now runs, the brief (2026-10-14) and the handoff (2026-10-13) are the current statements; the plan stays the only record of the ban report and of the sources checked by three reviewers.

Canonical for the Route A versus Route B decision and the reasoning on the Consumer Terms (a scheduled browser export is what they forbid). Its phases 1 to 5 and the 'about 300 lines' cost were deferred the next day and are stale; what the shared plane became is described by the brief and the handoff.

The only inventory of what cswap can export and import of a Project, with file and line citations at PR #45. Note its internal arithmetic (14,907 against parts summing 14,706), the PRIVACY.md version 16 that the same-day store runbook gives as 15, and that its memory-write question was never settled by a later artifact.

The only artifact on what each surface can do; checked 2026-10-03 and self-described as moving weekly. Its line that a claude.ai/code Project is 'a work organizer, not a knowledge base' is contradicted by the spec's export of a Code Project's instructions, memory and files five days later.

Canonical only for the listing texts, the privacy tab answers and the manifest facts of release 0.2.0.773. Its steps 7 and 8 (secrets in claude-swap-cloud, the in-repository release-kit script) are superseded by the handoff's symphony-extension location and the shared chrome-store-release-kit, and the Beethoven runbook of 2026-10-13 is the later description of the same automatic release path; the PyPI publish and the submission it waits on are not recorded as done anywhere in the cluster.

result.unsourced_summary: The cluster's load-bearing product facts are mostly sourced once and then repeated as settled. "A Project belongs to one user" is quoted from the Claude Code documentation only in the plan of 2026-10-08 (shared-multi-account-claude-project-plan); the primitives spec attributes it to an unshown "document 25", and the build plan and the student onboarding state it bare. "Branch protection on a private repository needs a paid plan" is linked to GitHub's page in the plan, then carried by the spec (via document 25 and move-gaps.md), the build plan (which says it is to be checked), the ladder and the store runbook, while the handoff later infers the organization is on Enterprise Cloud without reading a settings page. The routine caps (30 fires an hour per routine, 100 per account) rest on the plan's one link and are restated as "runs" by the build plan. The Consumer Terms are paraphrased in the plan, the spec, the build plan and the Slurm playbook with no quoted clause; the playbook's "pooling tokens is what the terms prohibit" and the plan's "grey zone" both lack a citation beyond a third-party ban report the plan itself marks unconfirmed, and the handoff's account-pool decision rests on the owner's word. Both Chrome Web Store runbooks assert Google OAuth lifetimes (refresh tokens from a Testing consent screen die after seven days; an unused client or token after six months), review times ("several days" against "one to three days"), that a lower version is refused, that Public can follow Unlisted without a new review, and that release runs never overlap, none with a page cited. The store runbook's Windows-double and macOS-tenfold multipliers and the ladder's 1.7x and 10x are both uncited at the sentence. The plan asserts without source that GitHub sends no event when main starts to conflict, that a Project with several repositories loads no hooks, and that MEMORY.md's 200 lines or 25 KB is "loaded at start". The brief's Cursor row is written from memory because cursor.com was blocked; its "closest relative is the C compiler experiment" and "most coding work is less parallel than research" are its own judgements. The taxonomy's six uniqueness claims are absence claims from a search that ran out of budget, and its risk 9 (Wayne State AI-tool approval, no BAA on a personal plan, Remote Control unavailable under HIPAA) carries no grade or source. The Slurm playbook's cluster generalities (compute nodes lack egress, home directories read-only, RHEL is what most clusters run, Unix sockets fail on Lustre, --overlap needed from Slurm 20.11, 429/529 retried with backoff) are stated as fact. The handoff names "the enterprise OpenGrid" with no file naming it and infers rather than measures that a routine's pull request is authored under the person's login.
result.stale_summary: Everything here is dated 3 to 15 October 2026 and self-labelled as of its day. The analysis and the playbook (2026-10-03) pin Claude Code version gates (v2.1.51, v2.1.183, v2.1.209, v2.1.221, v2.1.234, 2.1.271 pinned in the image), say Glob and Grep are "currently" out of the default tool set, that Code Projects are a public beta on Pro and Max, that retrieval mode's plan availability is unreconciled, and that Anthropic's documentation describes generating a setup token but not revoking one. The plan (2026-10-08) still has Linear as the queue, a routine as coordinator, an hourly schedule, "Pro and Max beta only", an untested bot-wakes-thread question and the unconfirmed February 2026 bans. The primitives spec and the store runbook (2026-10-08) wait on the PyPI publish (publish.yml not yet tagged, tag v0.27.0b1 to push), the first store submission, the memory write "never confirmed live", proactivity and PR-attribution keys "not verified", a never-captured cloud session id, and give PRIVACY.md as version 15 and 16 respectively. The build plan (2026-10-08, sized 2026-10-09) leaves the materializer, the thin Projects and the weekly export routine as phases that no later artifact reports built, and the several-accounts terms question unsettled. The ladder (2026-10-09) names sdlc-template, CLAUDE_WORKER=true, five unchecked setup items, Claude Enterprise pricing unverifiable, and says "the docs flag lags". The handoff and the Beethoven runbook (2026-10-13) list as pending: Beethoven 20.0.0's hand upload (dashboard images still 9.0.0's), beethoven-qa tags v4.0.0 and v5.0.0, submitting Symphony for Chrome and its CWS_ secrets, spine-program #72, deleting five test repositories, "every consumer on 0.4.1 and plugin 0.1.10" not rechecked against GitHub, GitHub Code Security not bought as of 2026-10-08, and the dated changes ahead: pull_request_target blocked on public repositories from 2026-11-02, the Usage Policy wording from 2026-11-12, ubuntu-latest to 26.04 in November 2026, REST API 2022-11-28 supported to about March 2028. The onboarding (2026-10-13) waits on issue 19 (can the grid reach GitHub), on whether the Project offers plugins, and gives CTSpinoPelvic1K v11 and the shared spineps212 path "unless the issue says otherwise". The brief (2026-10-14) and the taxonomy (2026-10-15) say nothing after 0.4.1 is released, eleven fixes sit on main, F8 waits on the owner, the deep lane #21 is unmerged, the canary is not adopted, the push-guard directory bug's fix is pending, the Phase 3 rails (run cap of 10, qa check, public runtime, control panel, account pool) are not built, the coordbench full run of 35 pairs chosen on 2026-10-15 is unreported, the extension is 20.0.0 pre-release, bare mode "will become" the default for claude -p, and the coordination experiment stays out of the grant text until the owner says otherwise.
result.notes: Twelve records read whole; the plain text of the plan, the spec, the build plan, the store runbook, the Beethoven runbook, the handoff, the brief, the analysis, the playbook, the ladder, the taxonomy and the onboarding was grepped where a record's quote was not enough. Quotes are copied from the records or the text files as they stand (including the records' own escaping); people are named by role. Two observations not listed as candidates: the taxonomy's "Symphony and Beethoven meet nowhere in code" (2026-10-15) sits beside the onboarding (2026-10-13), where a student's Beethoven session on the grid carries Symphony claims on spine-program, which is use together rather than a code integration, so it is not counted as a contradiction; and the brief's "50 pairs from 20 tasks" against the handoff's "flash 50" subset is left as a wording difference, since the handoff says 42 of those 50 grade. The clustering's single superseded relation holds with the caveat in canonical_check; the four canonical choices hold for their own subject, except the store runbook, whose release-path steps the handoff and the Beethoven runbook of 2026-10-13 overtake. Several figures are repeated between the handoff and the taxonomy because both read github/docs on consecutive days; they are listed once as duplicate-text. The CLAUDE.md context attached to this session was not used as a source for any candidate.

candidates.topic: How long a successor Slurm job can resume the same Remote Control session (--continue window): seven days or four hours
candidates.statement_a: The review (2026-10-21) says the successor job continues the same Remote Control session for up to seven days, and tables `claude remote-control --continue` within 7 days.
candidates.quote_a: On the grid a worker already survives the end of its job: the successor job continues the same Remote Control session for up to seven days, and the workspace stays on the shared disk.
candidates.statement_b: The plan (2026-10-07), reading hpcworker's code at e77863c, says the resume window is 14400 s (4 h), that four hours replaced seven days on purpose after Anthropic's statement, and that the seven-day text in hpcworker's CLAUDE.md and DIAGNOSTICS.md is stale.
candidates.quote_b: It adds `--continue` when `connection.json` is younger than `RESUME_WINDOW_S`, which defaults to 14400 s, 4 h (`framework/lib/profile_sh.sh:117`; template `:302-307`). The four hours replaced seven days on purpose, following Anthropic's statement that a session can be resumed "for about four hours" (`framework/README.md:1087-1088`; `docs/V11_CONTRACT.md:886`). The job's own preempted message also says four hours (`:415`). The seven days at `CLAUDE.md:265` is stale text.
candidates.why_it_matters: A planner who reads only the review would size job windows and queue waits on the assumption that a worker can be resumed after a day or more; the code reading says a successor that starts more than four hours after the last connection.json starts a fresh session. The review's own 'not measured yet' list admits --continue across several job ends is unmeasured, and it repeats the number the earlier plan flagged as stale.

candidates.topic: Whether a claude setup-token (CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN) may be injected into Slurm jobs on the grid
candidates.statement_a: The playbook (2026-10-03) makes a one-year setup token, stored 0600 on scratch and injected as CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN, the credential for every batch and non-interactive run.
candidates.quote_a: Use two credentials for two jobs. A one-year token from `claude setup-token`, minted on the laptop and stored on scratch, authenticates every batch and non-interactive run: it never needs refreshing, so a job that starts at 03:00 cannot fail on an expired access token.
candidates.statement_b: The roadmap (same day, 2026-10-03) rejects exactly that for Beethoven: injecting a setup-token or CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN into jobs is forbidden by the credential rule; the student's own claude auth login is used where it sits. The taxonomy spec (2026-10-15) restates the launcher as 'no API key and no setup-token'.
candidates.quote_b: `setup-token` or `CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN` injected into jobs (notes 07, 08, 09): forbidden by the credential rule; the student's `claude auth login` is used where it sits.
candidates.why_it_matters: The two artifacts from the same account on the same day give opposite credential models for the same cluster: a batch job built on the playbook's token-install.sh would break hpcworker's rule that Beethoven never reads, stores or relays a Claude credential, and the hpcworker launcher cannot open Remote Control on a setup token anyway (the playbook itself says Remote Control needs the /login credential).

candidates.topic: Whether several Claude accounts may be pooled or rotated to widen the usage window
candidates.statement_a: The playbook's compliance condition: one account per user, no account rotation, no pooled tokens; rotating accounts or pooling tokens to widen the window is what Anthropic's terms prohibit, and such a workload belongs on an API key.
candidates.quote_a: Keep it one account. Rotating accounts or pooling several users' tokens to widen the window is the behaviour Anthropic's terms prohibit; if the workload needs more than one subscription's window, it is a workload for an API key.
candidates.statement_b: The handoff (2026-10-13) records the owner's decision that the owner's own several Claude accounts may be coordinated from one orchestrator, designs an account pool of organization secrets picked by code, and describes cswap's failover switching between accounts when a window reaches 90 percent; the review (2026-10-21) then says workers.yml runs on 'the token pool' and the grid starts workers on 'Claude account slot N'.
candidates.quote_b: What the owner already decided. The owner's own several Claude accounts may be coordinated from one orchestrator of the owner's, each worker on one account's token, knowing the terms question. That decision does not change the rule for contributors: no contributor's credential and no pool of contributors' subscriptions.
candidates.why_it_matters: A planner reading the playbook would treat any multi-account pool as out of bounds; one reading the handoff and review would build on the pool. The handoff itself notes Anthropic's Usage Policy change of 2026-11-12 ('services that route requests through consumer subscriptions') and that enforcement could hit every pooled account at once, so the two positions must be reconciled before a benchmark or worker fleet is sized on pooled windows.

candidates.topic: The student's GitHub token for the grid: type, scope and file (onboarding versus the connect-the-grid guide, one day apart)
candidates.statement_a: Onboarding (2026-10-13): a fine-grained token with read access to Contents on spine-program only, saved as one line in $HOME/.beethoven/github_token, mode 600.

In your Beethoven session, save it as one line in $HOME/.beethoven/github\_token with mode 600.
candidates.statement_b: Connect the grid (2026-10-14): one classic token with the repo scope (read and write), 90-day expiry, stored in ~/.beethoven/git-credentials read by git's store helper; a fine-grained token is only the fallback and then needs Contents, Issues and Pull requests at Read and write, with a second token for the student's own repositories.
candidates.quote_b:
One classic token with the `repo` scope covers spine-program and your own repositories at once. [...] chmod 600 ~/.beethoven/git-credentials
git config --global credential.helper "store --file ~/.beethoven/git-credentials"
candidates.why_it_matters: A student following the onboarding page ends with a read-only token in a file git never reads, so the clone-and-push test in the later guide fails with 'Username for https://github.com'; a planner writing a job that reads $HOME/.beethoven/github_token finds nothing after the later guide is followed. The two pages also disagree on whether the token may write (push the claim branch) at all.

candidates.topic: What a Claude session may run on the login node
candidates.statement_a: The playbook's CLAUDE.md allows login-node work up to one CPU core for 60 seconds and 4 GB of memory, plus edit, inspect, submit and monitor.
candidates.quote_a: If it is not set, you are on a login node: edit, inspect, submit and monitor only. Never run anything that uses more than one CPU core for more than 60 seconds, loads a GPU, or exceeds 4 GB of memory on a login node. Submit it with sbatch instead.
candidates.statement_b: The lab recipe (2026-09-27), the onboarding (2026-10-13) and the roadmap (2026-10-03) give a stricter rule for Wayne State: the login node runs only sbatch, squeue, scancel, ls, tail and git; downloads are jobs too; 'Nothing runs on the login node: every computation, render, plot and download is a job, even a one-minute one'; hpcworker allows 'nothing on the login node beyond one sbatch, squeue or scancel per action'.
candidates.quote_b: The login node runs only `sbatch`, `squeue`, `scancel`, `ls`, `tail`, `git`. Downloads are jobs too; compute nodes have internet. | dozens of smoke tests on a node shared by \~95 users (2026-09-21)
candidates.why_it_matters: A worker steered by the playbook's CLAUDE.md would run one-minute tests and downloads on the login node that the lab's incident-backed rule forbids outright; the two rules cannot both be the one baked into a managed-settings image for this grid.

candidates.topic: Whether git works on the grid's login node
candidates.statement_a: The lab recipe lists git among the commands the login node runs, and its session-start routine does `git pull` on the grid.

candidates.quote_b: Run these commands in the terminal of your Beethoven session (a compute node), not on the login node, where git has not been tested yet.
candidates.why_it_matters: The SchwingNet pipeline's gate clones and fast-forwards ~/SchwingNet from the login node, so whether git survives there decides whether the gate route works at all; one artifact assumes it does, another treats it as untested with a kill symptom.

candidates.topic: Whether compute nodes have internet egress
candidates.statement_a: The playbook's first 'cluster fact' is that most compute nodes cannot reach the internet directly, so jobs must run on a partition with egress or through a proxy.
candidates.quote_a: Two cluster facts shape the design more than any Claude Code setting. First, most compute nodes cannot reach the internet directly; Claude Code needs `api.anthropic.com` on every turn, so the job must run on a partition with egress or through the site's HTTPS proxy.
candidates.statement_b: At Wayne State the compute nodes have internet: the student's Beethoven session cloned two public repositories from a compute node (2026-10-14), the lab recipe's rule 1 says 'compute nodes have internet', and the FluoroCap map says the grid's outbound IP is throttled by PMC (so it reaches out).
candidates.quote_b: Your Beethoven session already reaches GitHub: it cloned your two public repositories from the compute node. What it lacks is a login
candidates.why_it_matters: The playbook's site-discover.sh and egress probe are built around a limitation the local grid does not have; a planner importing the playbook's proxy design would add a moving part the lab's own measurements say is unneeded, while its token-on-login-node steps assume the opposite topology.

candidates.topic: Slurm dependency type for chained jobs: afterok versus afterany
candidates.statement_a: The pipeline page (2026-10-21) draws the start word's dependency graph with afterok edges (six of them) beside afterany ones.
candidates.quote_a: One word submits the whole graph with Slurm dependencies. The accented path is version 1, which no longer waits on the multi-day X-ray fetch. [...] afterok [...] afterok [...] afterany [...] afterok
candidates.statement_b: The lab recipe's grid rule 3 (and the roadmap's standing rule) is afterany, never afterok, because a time-limit kill made a whole chain DependencyNeverSatisfied on 2026-09-09.
candidates.quote_b: `--dependency=afterany`, never `afterok`; the child reads a file to decide whether the parent succeeded. | an 8 h limit made a whole chain DependencyNeverSatisfied (2026-09-09)
candidates.why_it_matters: If the SchwingNet chain uses afterok as drawn, a parent that hits its wall time (the X-ray fetch is a 4-day job, the catalog 12 h) leaves every dependent job DependencyNeverSatisfied, the exact failure the lab rule was written to prevent; the planner must check grid/*.sbatch rather than trust either page.

candidates.topic: How long an agent may poll or wait on the Slurm queue inside a session
candidates.statement_a: The lab recipe: no squeue loop beyond about ten minutes; an agent submits, estimates, checkpoints and stops, because polling burned a session limit four times on 2026-09-24.
candidates.quote_a: No `squeue` loop beyond about ten minutes: on 2026-09-24 polling agents burned a session limit four times in one day while the grid did the work.
candidates.statement_b: The playbook's CLAUDE.md: check at most once a minute, and for jobs under 20 minutes submit with sbatch --wait in a background command; its managed settings allow Monitor watches of up to 30 minutes.
candidates.quote_b: check at most once a minute and never in a tight loop. For jobs expected under 20 minutes, submit with `sbatch --wait` in a background Bash command and read the log when it returns.
candidates.why_it_matters: Both are rules handed to Claude; a worker under the playbook's rule can sit on the queue twice as long as the lab's incident-backed cap allows, spending the shared five-hour window the review and spec say several workers already crowd.

candidates.topic: What 'the gate' on the grid accepts: eight verbs, seven words, or the accounts words
candidates.statement_a: The plan (2026-10-07, hpcworker e77863c) says the gate takes one line of at most 200 bytes and only eight verbs: version, status, watch, connect, stop, restrict, read and forget; no verb can carry a prompt.

candidates.quote_b: Claude sends one gate word, and the answer comes back as a file Claude reads. [...] grid/gate.sh one word at a time records every job [...] output, at most 200 kB: branch grid of symphony-template, logs/job-schwingnet-<word>.json
candidates.why_it_matters: Three artifacts use 'the gate' for three vocabularies (the browser-key gate of framework 17, the grid-accounts ssh gate of framework 22, and SchwingNet's gate.sh); a planner scripting a word from one page against the gate of another gets a refusal, and the 200-byte line limit of one is easily confused with the 200 kB output cap of another.

candidates.topic: Gate limits on starting named workers: a hard cap of 3 names per 7 days versus only a 60-second floor
candidates.statement_a: At framework 17 the gate caps every caller at 3 worker names per 7 days, 12 connects per rolling hour and 2 watches at once, per account.

candidates.quote_b: Starting N workers takes about N minutes, because every start waits out the gate's 60 second floor | One word, `accounts start SLOT NAME COUNT`, makes COUNT workers in one call (names NAME-1 to NAME-COUNT), still one floor per call

candidates.topic: How many waiting runs a GitHub concurrency group keeps before cancelling
candidates.statement_a: One running and one waiting run; a newer waiting run replaces the older one.
candidates.quote_a: GitHub keeps at most one waiting run per concurrency group, so a third quick press of Start replaces the second one, which never runs.
candidates.statement_b: The spec's limits table gives a concurrency group 100 pending runs before the rest are cancelled.
candidates.quote_b: | A queue: max concurrency group | 100 pending runs; the rest are cancelled | The board's queue can overflow under a burst of events |
candidates.why_it_matters: The review's rank-1 fix (durable request files) rests on losing a press at the second waiting run; the spec's number would mean bursts of up to 100 are safe. Both cite GitHub's documentation without a line; they may describe two different limits, but a reader of either alone sizes the intake wrong.

candidates.topic: Whether a scheduled workflow can be relied on for periodic checks (the review's 15-minute list)
candidates.statement_a: Rank 4 proposes a scheduled list every 15 minutes to turn silent failures into visible ones.

candidates.statement_b: The handoff measured GitHub's schedules running hours late and dropping most slots (8 runs in about 300 ten-minute slots), and concludes every timing claim built on a cron does not hold.
candidates.quote_b: Schedules are best effort, and measured here they ran hours late and mostly not at all. Every timing claim built on a cron (the sweep 'within the hour', 'within about ten minutes', 'about half an hour later'; metrics at 03:43 'before the collector's read at 04:17') does not hold.
candidates.why_it_matters: A stale flag keyed to a 15-minute schedule would fire on GitHub's lateness rather than on a worker's silence; the handoff's measurement says the review's fix needs an event trigger or a longer threshold.

result.unsourced_summary: The cluster's operating picture rests on several claims that no artifact measures or cites. The review (2026-10-21) and the handoff (2026-10-13) both reason from a 90-minute limit on a cloud Claude worker without saying where it comes from, while the taxonomy spec's limits table gives a job six hours. Connect-the-grid and the onboarding both warn that the hpcworker framework empties its run folders, with no file or incident cited, while the plan of 2026-10-07 says the new client deletes nothing. The playbook, the taxonomy spec (risk 9) and the plan of 2026-10-07 all build on Remote Control needing a claude.ai subscription sign-in, and the spec adds that Remote Control stores transcripts at Anthropic and is unavailable under a HIPAA configuration, with no grade or source. The review, the one-per-project plan and the plan of 2026-10-07 all describe or depend on a successor job continuing the same Remote Control session with --continue, and all three say it is unmeasured. The review and the spec assert that several workers on one account share the five-hour window and stall together, from the plan's structure rather than a test, the spec's one observation being interactive threads. Single-artifact assertions a planner would also take as given: the review's 'no port is open on the grid', 'GitHub never holds a Claude credential' and 'most hosted agent platforms run on their own vendor's machines'; the one-per-project plan's premise that a claude.ai project reaches a worker only through Work locally and that the environment id is stable per machine id; the playbook's 'most compute nodes cannot reach the internet directly' and 'Unix sockets do not work on Lustre or NFS'; the onboarding's 'three refused codes lock you out for fifteen minutes' and 'about two business days' for a grid account; the FluoroCap map's 'the grid's outbound IP is captcha-throttled by PMC' against the access setup's 'publishers authenticate by IP'; the RDP runbook's 'Windows Home cannot host Remote Desktop', 'a sleeping P50 drops off Tailscale' and the P50's CPU generation; and the review's and spec's GitHub concurrency-group behaviour (one waiting run versus 100 pending), each attributed to GitHub's documentation without a line.
result.stale_summary: Dated state that has likely moved by 2026-10-22: the review's grid state is 'read at 12:03 UTC, 21 Oct' (framework 22, one worker on hao1, account 1 signed in, no second worker started, rank 6 designed never built, the Beethoven Connect failure parked, the owner's choice among ten fixes open); the one-per-project plan (2026-10-21 20:06 UTC request) awaits the owner's go, needs a store release on Beethoven 23.x, and says 'today' only the Wayne State Max account is signed in on the grid. The SchwingNet pipeline page (2026-10-21) has the gate words under review in PR #54, zero grid jobs run, one owner press (Connect GitHub Actions after beethoven-extension #23) outstanding, 15 of 20 bank recipes 'to confirm', 22 training entries without a shard, the RSNA RATIC link expiring 2026-10-28 02:38 UTC, VinDr-PCXR access granted 21 Oct, and milestones from 23 Oct to the 30 Oct provisional and 2 Nov talk. Connect-the-grid: write access 'checked 2026-10-14', a 90-day token (lapsing about 2027-01-12), git 'not tested yet' on the login node, and archive links that 'point at nothing' until the owner's script runs. The onboarding (2026-10-13) still routes files through a laptop 'until issue 19 settles', quotes Pro at about US$20 a month and the archive move 'since 2026-10-13'. The playbook and the Chat-versus-Code analysis were checked against Anthropic's documentation on 2026-10-03, with version gates (v2.1.51, v2.1.183, v2.1.208/228, v2.1.233), a pinned 2.1.271 (the image build of 2026-10-07 installs 2.1.283, the action of 2026-10-09 2.1.296), a one-year setup token, no documented revocation, and weekly caps 'introduced in August 2025'; the handoff flags Anthropic's Usage Policy change on 2026-11-12 and pull_request_target's default block on 2026-11-02. The RDP runbook (2026-09-27) hinges on Windows 10 extended support ending 2026-10-13, now past, with Duo ending Windows 10 support the same month. The lab recipe's gap table is 'What is not yet true (2026-09-27)' (167 bare numerals, 0 of 79 manifest keys with a job id, public mirror still v10). The plan of 2026-10-07 is 'Deferred' at 22:33Z, reads hpcworker at framework 17 while saying the live version is not established (resolved as 22 by the review), cites hub SEAMS.md as out of date, and flags the seven-day resume text as stale in three files. The roadmap (2026-10-03) reads framework 11 and extension 12.0.0 with six owner decisions open. The encapsulation report's header still says two pull requests are open while its body says they merged 2026-10-07, and the website renders VS Code terms version 5 against main's 7. The taxonomy spec (2026-10-15) and brief (2026-10-14) have release 0.4.1 as the latest, F8 waiting on the owner, the deep lane #21 unmerged, the 10-runs-a-day cap 'not built', extension 20.0.0 pre-release, beethoven-qa 5.0.0 untagged past v3.0.0, and coordbench's 50-pair run not yet run; the handoff (2026-10-13) says its own claims were not rechecked against GitHub and lists Beethoven 20.0.0 to the store and beethoven-qa tags v4.0.0 and v5.0.0 as pending. The FluoroCap pages (2026-09-14) say a refetch 'is running now', cite a library note of 30 June 2026 on DMC residents' access, and were generated from a repository commit of that day.
result.notes: Records read whole for all seventeen members; plain texts consulted for the quotes above (review, one-per-project plan, connect-the-grid, playbook, RDP runbook, pipeline, onboarding, lab recipe, the plan of 2026-10-07, roadmap, encapsulation, spec, handoff, brief, Chat-versus-Code, FluoroCap map and access setup). A sentence-level and 12-word-shingle scan across all seventeen texts found no large verbatim reuse; the duplicate-text candidates are short shared formulations. Names in quotes were replaced by '[the owner]'; the student's GitHub login, which appears in the connect-the-grid text, is not reproduced. Several of the contradictions are between a site-agnostic playbook and the lab's own rules (login-node use, compute-node egress, scratch paths, polling), which an experiment planner would otherwise merge into one rule set; the resume-window, credential-model and account-pooling disagreements are the three most consequential for a worker fleet. The 'gate' ambiguity (browser-key gate of framework 17 with eight verbs; the grid-accounts ssh gate of framework 22 with accounts words; SchwingNet's gate.sh with seven words) is likely three different gates rather than one disagreement, but no artifact says so. Not raised as candidates because they describe different systems rather than one quantity: hpcworker's default worker (2 CPUs, 8G, 8 h, renewal every 8 h), VS Code's (4 CPUs, 16G, 24 h), and the playbook's interactive (4 h, 4 CPUs, 16G) and workspace (8 h) jobs. The clustering gives no superseded or duplicate relations, so canonical_check records how each canonical member stands against the records and proposes one superseded relation (onboarding superseded by connect-the-grid on the student's login). The repository's own memory index (outside the artifact set) states that the template now vendors symphony-protocol 0.5.0 and that Beethoven 21.0.0 exists; those are pointers for re-checking the brief's and spec's release state, not findings from the records.

canonical_check.why: It is the only audit of the sealed-repository standard across the seven repositories and carries the measured test counts; but its one open decision (VS Code's grid scripts) was taken the same evening in the VS Code plan, and its header predates its own body on the agents and research merges, so the VS Code plan's status line and the pull-request table override it on those two points.

It is the one statement of the six phases and gates; its starting point (framework 11, nothing headless, no gates, two repositories) is dated 2026-10-03 and is superseded in substance by the encapsulation report (seven repositories), the spec (splits.py exists, Metaflow chosen) and the grid review (framework 22), none of which the clustering lists as superseding it.

It is the only item-by-item mapping of REFORMS to gates; its 'none exists yet', 'proposed beethoven-research' and open questions are stale by 2026-10-07 and 2026-10-15, and its same-day sibling, the roadmap, disagrees on whether the mapping was checked against the paper.

It is the release runbook for the Beethoven item; the clustering lists no duplicate though its section 2 (OAuth client, refresh token, five CWS_ secrets, CWS_ON_PUSH) is the same procedure as the store-upload runbook's steps 7 and 8 for the sibling extension, which it says to reuse.

The clustering gives duplicates: []; the two runbooks share the kit, the OAuth Playground steps, the five secrets, the variable and the four-part build number nearly line for line, and the Beethoven runbook tells the owner to reuse the client and refresh token made for the other repository.

The clustering gives superseded: []; on the framework version live on the grid the review (framework 22, measured 2026-10-21) supersedes the VS Code plan's 'not established (10, 13, 15, 16 or 17)' and the roadmap's framework 11, while on the resume window the review repeats the seven days the VS Code plan showed to be stale text, so the supersession runs one way only on the version.

result.unsourced_summary: The cluster's design rests on a handful of statements that no member measures or cites. The grid's constraints are taken from hpcworker's own CLAUDE.md, not from the node: the roadmap and the REFORMS checklist both say the login node is CentOS 7 with bash 4.2 and Python 3.6, which is the whole reason the gates split three ways and heavy Python goes to the container, and the VS Code plan admits its shell checks ran under bash 5.2.21. The roadmap states that Wayne State is CephFS with a Panasas home with no source, and the lab recipe only implies it (a CephFS volume, pan_quota). The playbook's cluster generalities (most compute nodes have no internet, home is often read-only, Unix sockets fail on Lustre and NFS, the base matches the RHEL family most clusters run) are stated without sources and the first is contradicted by the lab recipe's site rule. On credentials and sessions: that Anthropic stores Remote Control transcripts appears in the taxonomy spec with no grade and in the VS Code plan sourced only to hpcworker's own notice; that a cloud worker stops at 90 minutes is asserted by the grid review and the Symphony handoff with no measurement, and it sizes the ten-runs-a-day cap; that framework 22 runs several named workers at once is read from code in the several-workers plan while the same day's review says no second worker has ever been started; the seven-day resume in the grid review is the figure the VS Code plan showed to be stale text. On REFORMS: the 32/20/12 split is the checklist author's classification of 2026-10-03, which the roadmap of the same day says was not checked against the paper, and the taxonomy spec carries it as a property of beethoven-research. On the store: both runbooks give the seven-day and six-month refresh-token lifetimes, the review durations (one to three days, several days), the 'store refuses a lower version' rule and 'Google does not verify apps with the write scope' with no citation. On GitHub: the store-upload runbook's Free-or-Team quota and the handoff's Enterprise Cloud are each inferred, not read from a settings page. Smaller unsourced shared claims: a DOI cannot be withdrawn (checklist), the framework empties hpcworker's run folders (connect-the-grid), three refused grid codes lock a student out for fifteen minutes and a grid account takes about two business days (onboarding).
result.stale_summary: Dated states that have moved by 2026-10-22: the roadmap and the REFORMS checklist (2026-10-03) describe hpcworker at framework 11 and the extension at 12.0.0, two repositories, no gates and no beethoven-research; by 2026-10-07 the encapsulation report seals seven repositories and beethoven-research exists, by 2026-10-15 the spec reports splits.py built and Metaflow chosen, and by 2026-10-21 the grid answers framework 22 and Beethoven is 23.x. The roadmap's six owner decisions and the checklist's three open questions are recorded nowhere as answered except decision 3 (the third repository exists) and, in the spec, decision 2 (Metaflow); phase 0's probe, the headless run and the outer loop are not reported built, while phase 5's store release happened on 2026-10-13. The encapsulation report (2026-10-07) still lists the VS Code decision as open and its header still says two pull requests are open; the VS Code plan's status line of 22:33Z that day records the deferral. The VS Code plan is pinned to beethoven-vscode 631226e and hpcworker e77863c, says the live framework version is not established (10, 13, 15, 16 or 17), carries Claude Code 2.1.283 in the image build, dates the relay and ssh timings to 2026-09-28, and lists a dozen behaviours 'not yet measured' (two Remote Control hosts on one sign-in, --continue across a renewal, a claude -p beside remote-control, GPU jobs, the pilot student's end-to-end check); the grid review of 2026-10-21 still lists --continue across job ends and two workers at once as unmeasured. The Chrome runbook (2026-10-13) says 'upload 20.0.0 now', the dashboard images are 9.0.0's, CWS_ON_PUSH stays unset until then and the release.yml pull request is not yet merged; the handoff of the same day lists the 20.0.0 upload, the beethoven-qa v4.0.0 and v5.0.0 tags and beethoven-vscode #11 and #12 as the owner's pending steps; nothing in the cluster records any of them done, and the extension is at 23.x needing another store release. The store-upload runbook (2026-10-08) describes Beethoven as published Private with a testers' group, retired on 2026-10-13, and waits on a PyPI publisher and tag v0.27.0b1. The onboarding (2026-10-13) sends students to the retired testers group, treats the grid's reach to GitHub as unsettled (settled from a compute node on 2026-10-14) and the archive as populated (the next day's guide says the links point at nothing); the connect-the-grid guide says git is untested on the login node while the lab recipe of 2026-09-27 lists git among the login node's allowed commands. The taxonomy spec and manual are 'verified as of 2026-10-15' with beethoven-qa 5.0.0 untagged at v3.0.0 and the extension 20.0.0 pre-release. The playbook's facts were checked against Anthropic's documentation on 2026-10-03 with a 2.1.271 example pin and version-gated features. The lab recipe's gap table is 'what is not yet true (2026-09-27)' (167 bare numerals, 0 of 79 manifest keys with a job id, the public mirror still v10, no imaging repository on Nextflow).
result.notes: Dates are from each record's header or body. People are named by role; the owner's first name inside quoted text is replaced by [the owner]. Things checked and found consistent, so not listed: hpcworker offers six exports (contract, contract-text, profiles, module-schema, testbed, framework) and the extension takes five of them, which matches the VS Code plan's 'six exports'; the access service's move to beethoven-access on 2026-10-07 is told the same way by the encapsulation report and the VS Code plan; the 60-second scheduler floor is repeated by the roadmap, the VS Code plan, the grid review and the playbook ('at most once a minute') without conflict; the REFORMS citations differ in form (Kapoor et al. 2024; arXiv 2308.07832; Science Advances 2024 with DOI) but name one work. Two '5 of the 9 agent markers' findings (the mock portal in the encapsulation report, VS Code's grid/beethoven in the VS Code plan) concern different components and are not treated as a duplicate. The Chrome runbook's permission list carries no nativeMessaging although the extension has a native bridge; the runbook also says the store package holds no bridge/, .msi or .pkg, so the bridge ships outside the store and this was not raised as a contradiction. Whether the claude-swap-cloud runbook's extension is the symphony-extension the Beethoven runbook tells the owner to reuse the OAuth client from is not established in the records and was not assumed. SchwingNet's project files (not artifacts) say beethoven-qa 6.0.0 is awaited, one more step in the version chain recorded here only from the artifacts (2.0.0, 3.0.0 tag, 5.0.0 main). The embedded figures in the roadmap, the grid review and the spec could not be read.

candidates.quote_a: 802 CT records annotated and openly released ... 2 permanent archives: a Zenodo DOI and a public dataset mirror
candidates.statement_b: The CTSpinoPelvic1K release v11, with a dataset article, on Zenodo and Hugging Face. No link or DOI is given.
candidates.quote_b: CTSpinoPelvic1K release v11, the dataset article, Zenodo and Hugging Face
candidates.why_it_matters: Applications are told to cite the released dataset as OSC's record, but neither artifact gives its DOI, release version or record count from the archive. The 802 cannot be checked from either page.

candidates.topic: Size of OSC's released CT dataset (possible: neither record says the three numbers describe one release)
candidates.statement_a: 802 CT records openly released.
candidates.quote_a: 802 CT records annotated and openly released
candidates.statement_b: The public labelled CT arm counted from the sacrum uses 801 abdominopelvic spines. The onboarding names the release CTSpinoPelvic1K, a name that suggests about a thousand.
candidates.quote_b: From the sacrum: 6,234/6,255 (99.66%) on 801 abdominopelvic spines
candidates.why_it_matters: If the 801-spine arm, the CTSpinoPelvic1K release and the 802 'records' are the same set, an application citing 802 should agree with the archive's own count. If they differ, the reason should be stated before the number goes into an application.

candidates.topic: Whether OSC's actual outreach fits SAFB (on campus, free and open to the public)
candidates.statement_a: SAFB, the one event fund, requires an event on campus, free and open to the public for its whole length. The page treats OSC outreach as an annotation workshop or Zoom session.
candidates.quote_a: the event must be on campus and free and open to the public for its whole duration . A Zoom-based annotation session for enrolled trainees may not qualify at all.
candidates.statement_b: The OSC outreach event on the flyers is a soccer night at the off-campus Detroit City Fieldhouse, for children under 18 with a named condition only, and food must be bought at the venue.
candidates.quote_b: Every kid under 18 living with scoliosis or a spine condition ... Detroit City Fieldhouse
candidates.why_it_matters: The funding record calls Celebrate Life 'an OSC outreach event of the kind this briefing seeks to fund'. Under the page's own SAFB rule, an off-campus night limited to one patient group does not qualify, and none of the twelve sources is checked against this kind of event.

candidates.topic: Who hosts OSC outreach events
candidates.statement_a: OSC is not a Registered Student Organization; an existing registered organization should host the event with OSC as the programme.
candidates.quote_a: The fastest way around that is to have an existing registered organization host the event with OSC as the program, rather than registering OSC itself.
candidates.statement_b: The flyers present the event with Detroit City FC (or the Fieldhouse) and the OpenSpine Consortium, with a club staff contact and the owner as contacts, and name no student organization.
candidates.quote_b: [a club staff contact], Detroit City FC ... @openspineconsortium
candidates.why_it_matters: Sources that require a registered student organization (SAFB, the alumni funds via Student Affairs) cannot fund the event as the flyers present it. A host organization would have to be added before applying.

canonical_check.why: The two records describe the same event: same Saturday, October 24, same Detroit City Fieldhouse, same two contacts, same registration form ([the registration form's link]) and same event page. Several lines are copied word for word. The export's README calls noutom 'the first Celebrate Life flyer'; julcos is the only other one and is fuller (hours, food rule, watch party, the 'everyone plays' rule). Neither flyer says it replaces the other, so the order rests on the README, not on a dated statement. The rewrite also changed the audience (pediatric hematology/oncology to scoliosis and spine conditions), the time (6:45 PM kickoff to 5:00-7:00 PM), the companion event (outdoor Trunk or Treat to indoor Turf or Treat) and the food promise. The julcos record notes it did not read noutom. Superseded is right for the flyer, but the audience change is undocumented, and the old flyer still points at the live form.

result.unsourced_summary: Funding page (SchwingNet/osc-outreach-funding-kak2gk): the funder amounts and deadlines are attributed to the funders' own sites by domain only (read in September 2026), and four entries are marked as leads. What has no source at all: OSC's record to cite in every application (802 CT records released, 13 medical students trained, two permanent archives), with no dataset DOI or link given; only the Cureus paper (doi:10.7759/cureus.112661) is cited. Also unsourced: that OSC is not a Registered Student Organization; that the resident cannot apply for 'any student award' (AIDaS ties a narrower version, PI eligibility, to its own call); that a research year 'usually' keeps enrolment; and the $70,000 Community Foundation precedent, credited to 'Wayne State news coverage' with no link. Onboarding (SchwingNet/spine-program-student-onboarding) says the dataset is on Zenodo and Hugging Face as CTSpinoPelvic1K v11, also without a link. Neither artifact lets a reader check the 802 count, and the AIDaS draft's 801 abdominopelvic spines may or may not be the same set. Flyers (SchwingNet/celebrate-life-flyer-noutom and SchwingNet/celebrate-life-scoliosis-night-julcos): every operational promise is the organiser's own statement with no confirming source. That covers the professional coaches from Southeast Michigan (identical text in both), the simultaneous Halloween event (named and staged differently in each), the under-18 eligibility, food provided (first) versus no outside food (second), and the post-event watch party. AIDaS (SchwingNet/aidas-seed-grant-proposal) adds unsourced hardware prices, a $24/h annotation rate and the Joint Commission count; the onboarding adds unsourced student costs (Claude Pro about US$20 a month, paid by the student) and timings.
result.stale_summary: Both Celebrate Life flyers are dated only 'Saturday, October 24', with no year. October 24, 2026 is a Saturday, two days after 2026-10-22, so both expire then. The first flyer (noutom, 6:45 PM kickoff, oncology audience) is already replaced by the scoliosis flyer (julcos, 5:00-7:00 PM) but still points at the same live registration form and event page. The funding page (osc-outreach-funding-kak2gk) was written in September 2026, and much of it has moved. RSNA's 2026-27 cycles are 'closed' and open 'next month' (October 2026), so they should be open now. Its pre-October steps (settle RSNA membership and the departmental match) are past due. 'The one thing to do this week' (confirm enrolment, ask Student Affairs about alumni funds) dates from September, and any three-day fast path from a recent abstract acceptance has lapsed. The 2026-27 GME and Senate cycles, and the future deadlines (1 February and 13 March for RSNA and SIR, 16 Feb 2027 for AOA), all need re-checking. The OSC record counts (802 records, 13 students, one 2026 paper) are a September snapshot. The AIDaS proposal's submission deadline of October 16, 2026 has passed, with no record of submission; its faculty PI, department, collaborator agreement and budget lines 1-5 are still 'to confirm', and the manuscript is still 'in preparation'. The student onboarding is dated 2026-10-13, and its laptop-shipping step waits on issue 19.
result.notes: I worked only from the five records and three plain texts. People are named by role. Quotes leave out the printed contact names, the venue's street address, e-mails and phone numbers, so some quotes are partial (marked with '...'). Three candidates are internal to the funding page (artifact_a equals artifact_b) because they bear directly on 'in what order'. The dataset-size candidate (802 versus 801 abdominopelvic spines versus the name CTSpinoPelvic1K) is marked as possible, since no record says these are one release. Other things worth knowing that did not make a candidate: (1) The funding page's '13 medical students trained as annotators' and the onboarding's '13 numbered project folders' are different quantities that happen to share a number; the funding record's related_titles links them loosely. (2) The AIDaS seed grant ($20,000, faculty PI required, research rather than outreach, deadline passed) is not among the funding page's twelve sources, and its budget pays for a graduate student annotator rather than the volunteer medical-student annotators the funding page cites. (3) AIDaS says the new DMC fluoroscopy corpus will not be released publicly, so it cannot add to the 'openly released' record that the outreach applications cite. (4) The onboarding has students paying for Claude Pro themselves; the funding page says only the resident-held GME Seed Grant pays for software. (5) The first flyer's HTML holds 2026-07-29 only inside a runtime JavaScript comment; neither flyer prints a year.
